growth.why_this_wins: Fresh July 2026 NASA/Nature science creates a real new angle on a proven evergreen curiosity topic. The story has a strong beauty-versus-infrastructure paradox, broad audience appeal, a clear 8–10 minute consequence ladder, and unusually strong visual grammar for the proven doodle renderer.
growth.core_paradox: The most beautiful visible effect of the storm can arrive alongside invisible stress on satellites, navigation, radio and long electrical conductors.
growth.hook_promise: Start with auroras spreading far beyond the poles, then reveal what an extreme Earth-directed solar storm would actually break, what would survive, and why a new 2026 result makes the worst case less settled than scientists thought.
critic_lessons_applied: Do not use generic apocalypse claims.
Every section must introduce a new mechanism, consequence, contrast or payoff.
Use the 2026 science as a fresh twist, not as clickbait proof of unlimited damage.
Prefer explanatory diagrams and character actions over decorative slides.

research_questions: How should flare, energetic-particle and CME effects be separated for viewers?
Which modern systems are directly vulnerable versus secondarily dependent on power or communications?
What does the July 2026 NASA-led Nature result actually establish and what remains uncertain?
Which historical cases are strong enough to anchor the consequence chain without sensationalism?
fact_risks: Do not claim guaranteed worldwide blackout.
Do not describe geomagnetic storms as an EMP that fries every consumer electronic device.
Do not claim a fixed warning time or recovery duration without scenario-specific evidence.
Use cautious language for the 2026 non-saturation result and extreme-event extrapolation.
